title: In-Memory Folder Tree
statement:
Build a tiny file system that lives in memory. Paths are absolute, like "/docs/todo": a leading /, then names of lowercase letters separated by /. The path "/" alone is the root folder.

  • MemoryFS() starts with an empty root folder.
  • listDir(path): if path is a file, return a list with just that file's name. If it is a folder, return the names of everything directly inside it, files and folders together, sorted in lexicographic order.
  • makeDir(path) creates the folder, along with any missing folders on the way. Creating a folder that already exists does nothing.
  • appendText(path, text) adds text to the end of a file's content. If the file does not exist, create it (and any missing folders above it) with text as its content.
  • readText(path) returns the full content of a file.

Calls are always valid: listDir and readText name paths that exist (and readText names a file), no folder is ever created where a file is, and no file is ever created where a folder is.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the file system. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Listing a folder shows folders and files together. Listing a file returns only its own name, not the folder's contents.
The first append creates the folders a and b and the file. The second append adds to the end instead of replacing.
The listing is sorted by name, not by the order things were created.

constraints: Names use only lowercase English letters
hints: A path is a sequence of names. Which structure stores many sequences that share prefixes, the way folders share parents?
Make each folder a node whose children sit in a map from name to node. A file is a node with content instead of children.
Walk the path one name at a time, creating missing nodes when writing. listDir on a folder sorts its children's names; on a file it returns the last name of the path.

explain.intuition:
A folder tree is a trie whose edges are whole names instead of single letters. Each node keeps a map from child name to child node. To reach "/docs/todo", start at the root and follow docs, then todo. Writing operations create nodes they don't find; reading operations can assume the path exists.

A file is just a node that also holds text. The only branch in the logic is listDir: a folder answers with its sorted child names, a file answers with its own name. This is the same shape as a DOM tree or a router's nested routes: walk segment by segment from the root.
steps: Helper walk(path, create): split on /, drop empty parts, and step from the root through each name, creating missing nodes if create is set.
appendText: walk(path, true), mark the node as a file, append the text.
readText: return the node's content. listDir: if the node is a file, return the last name in the path; otherwise return the sorted child names.
pitfalls: Splitting "/" into ["", ""] and creating a folder with an empty name. Filter out empty parts.
Returning the parent folder's listing when listDir gets a file path. It must return only that file's name.
Replacing the content on append instead of adding to the end.

complexity.time: O(path length) per call, plus O(k log k) to sort k names in listDir
complexity.space: O(total length of all paths and text)

solutions.title: Map of full paths
solutions.idea: Store every folder and file under its full path string. Each folder keeps a set of its children's names; creating a path registers every prefix.
solutions.time: O(path length) per call, O(k log k) for listDir

solutions.title: Trie of names
solutions.idea: Each node maps child names to child nodes. Walk the path from the root one name at a time; a file is a node that carries text.
solutions.time: O(path length) per call, O(k log k) for listDir

followups: Add delete(path) that removes a file or a whole folder. What has to change in each design?
listDir is called far more often than makeDir. How would you avoid sorting on every call?
Support relative paths with ".." and ".". Where in the code does that logic belong?
